You’re entering crunch time (and I’m not talking about finals here). The transi-
tion to the “working world” is not easily negotiated. The sexual landscape is
littered with land mines, even for those of us who are seeking to honor Christ,
and a major life transition often arouses the anxiety, uncertainty, and isolation
that for many are triggers for lust and sexual sin.
The smells of spring were intoxicating. The winter rains had come and
gone. It was the perfect time for an attack—after the torrential down-
pours and before the backbreaking work of the harvest. It was the time
that the general/king knew from years of hardened experience that
he must go on the offensive if he were to carry out the mission of his
Creator/King.
Yet he remained at home in the comforts of his palace while sending
his men to fight the enemy on his behalf. We aren’t given details of
what was going on in his head. Perhaps he believed his faithful com-
mander could handle the job without him. Perhaps he was tired from
years of battle—the blood, pain, and death. Perhaps he was simply
being lazy. Or perhaps he had made small choices over the preceding
weeks that had dulled his God-given conscience about the need to fol-
low the orders of his King.
Because he was king, no one questioned his decision, at least not to his
face. He spent his days enjoying the trappings of being rich and power-
ful. He slept. He ate. He played. He carried out his duties in relative
peace and quiet. And he even attempted to worship as was his custom.
God, however, seemed distant. Every time he tried to get close, he had
a gnawing sense that God desired for him to be in a different place. If
at that point he had stopped and been honest with himself, he would
have become aware that he was not doing what he had been called
and created to do as a representative of the Creator/King on earth.
Yawn. The good life, while comfortable, was getting old and boring. He
got up from his bed and decided to go to one of his favorite spots—the
roof of his palace. He loved spending time there in solitude, away from
the hustle and bustle. This was where he poured out his heart to the
Lord and where God spoke to his innermost being. On this night, how-
ever, there weren’t songs of praise flowing from his heart and lips. He
felt bored. He felt tired in a lethargic sort of way. He felt an uncomfort-
able aimlessness.
The breath went right out of him. In the darkness, even from the roof,
he could tell that the woman he saw bathing was physical beauty incar-
nate. Something powerful grabbed his heart. The pull was overwhelm-
ing. Intoxicated with lust, he schemed of ways that he might “have
her.” His mood turned euphoric with the thought that, as king, he
could pull it off.
The ancient story spares us the details of their late-night rendezvous.
We get the picture. We need not imagine the scene in the palace
that night. It is clear, however, that the great king, his passion gone
wild, would live with the consequences for the rest of his life. And so
would countless others. His lust would ultimately lead to murder and
the shame of an entire kingdom. The toll on his life and the lives of so
many others would be devastating. What went wrong? How could this
giant of a man, courageous, loving, and spiritual, be responsible for
such heartache and pain?
This is one of the Bible’s most famous stories. David’s unfettered lust
connection with Bathsheba found in 2 Samuel 11—12 remains one
of the most shocking tragedies involving one of God’s great heroes.
David was the model king of the Old Testament. He was the only one
of whom it has been said that he was “a man after [God’s] own heart”
(1 Samuel 13:14, NIV). Who can read the Psalms, dripping with spiritual
passion and desire, without recognizing the deep intimacy and friend-
ship David enjoyed with God? To dissect this story would be time well
spent. For now, however, let this episode in biblical history ring in our
ears and our hearts. Bottom line: If this kind of shipwreck could happen
to a guy like David, it could happen to you or me.
You’re entering crunch time (and I’m not talking about finals here). The
transition to the “working world” is not easily negotiated. For most of
us, our time as undergrads provides the opportunity to have access to a
close-knit Christian community. I’ve found that campus life, though full
of outrageous temptations, not the least of which are sexual in nature,
fosters a lifestyle where deep relationships with other believers are not
unusual. As you enter the marketplace, there will be new and intense
challenges. The stresses of life will pull you, sometimes imperceptibly,
away from kingdom living. It will take great intention to continue to
pursue Christ as your treasure when many around you will be looking
for the Promised Land in an assortment of other pastures.
As with David (and you can mention other biblical characters like Sam-
son and Solomon here too), the sexual landscape is littered with land
mines even for those of us who are seeking to honor Christ. When re-
ferring to the topic of sexuality in this article, I mean to encompass our
thought life regarding prospective encounters with sexuality: that to
which we are commonly exposed in the media (including the Internet)
and in our relationships with those of the opposite sex.
My hunch is that I don’t need to sell you on the fact that God treats
our sexuality seriously—for many reasons. When we sin sexually, we
sin against our own bodies. Sexual sin damages our most important
relationships, not the least of which is the marriage bond—a mirror of
Christ’s relationship with His bride, the church. Sexual sin often takes
on a life of its own and can quickly spin out of control. Sexual sin is a
form of idolatry, taking what was created and using it as a substitute
for what only God can fill, whether it is in the form of pixels, romance
novels, chat rooms, or sexually immoral relationships. Perhaps more
than any other, it is an area of life that produces great shame and guilt.
When it comes to controlling ourselves sexually, the stakes are high.
But let’s stop and catch our breath. I’d like to offer some hope here. It
is possible to live in sexual integrity. It is possible to walk the journey of
progressive victory over lust and sexual temptation. And even more im-
portant is the hope that our sexual temptation can lead us into deeper
intimacy with Christ and the opportunity to experience His life-giving
presence in significant ways.

A FRESH
LOOK AT
AN ANCIENT
PRINCIPLE
God’s Word has much to say about personal and sexual purity (see
Psalm 51:10; Proverbs 15:16; Matthew 5:8; 15:16; Mark 7:21; Romans
13:13; 1 Corinthians 6:18; 10:8; 2 Corinthians 6:6; Philippians 1:10; 2:15;
4:8; Colossians 3:5; 1 Timothy 1:5; 4:12; 2 Timothy 2:22; Hebrews 13:4).
I’d like to introduce a phrase that I’ve found helpful in creating an en-
vironment in which we can experience freedom in the sexual area of
our lives. The principle of sexual integrity, while honoring the biblical
pursuit of purity, creates a context by which we move toward the Lord
in relationship. Here are a couple of examples of how integrity can be
defined: “The quality of being honest and morally upright.” “Moral
soundness, honesty, freedom from corrupting influence or motive.”
Note the emphasis I’ve placed on honesty in the definitions above. We
can say that honesty—“walking in the light,” to use biblical language
(1 John 1)—is the context through which we move toward sexual in-
tegrity. In fact, as you move into the marketplace, the foundation for
success in honoring God sexually will be your willingness and intention
to be honest and to walk in the light with God and others.
LIVING IN THE
LIGHT—WHAT IT
LOOKS LIKE
Sexual sin and lust are primarily results of a deficiency in the way we relate
in deep ways to God and others. We click on a suggestive website, chat
with someone we don’t know online, get hooked into romance novels and
TV shows, or let our minds run wild with fantasy because we are look-
ing for real connection. While there’s no question that God places moral
requirements on His children, at the end of the day we need to think about
sin as a relational issue. I reach toward the “drug” of lust or sex because
there is a relational need that is going unmet in my life.
Think about an alcoholic for a moment. At a certain point he realizes that
alcohol is destroying his life. Yet he still is powerless to stop drinking. To
tell him that getting drunk is wrong and that he shouldn’t do it won’t
help him stop. He needs a real connection with God and others to give
him the power to stop drinking.
If our problem with sexual sin is primarily about connecting with God and
others, so is the solution. This is why it is so important for us to walk in
the light, immersing ourselves in a community of others who are pursuing
Christ. The Bible speaks about the importance of friendship and how with
it we are stronger than without it (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Most importantly,
it means that we need to express and even embrace our powerlessness
and weakness before God and moment by moment surrender to Him
It is not bad or wrong to be weak. In fact, the Bible expresses clearly that it
is only in our weakness that we can experience the reality of Christ’s power
in us (2 Corinthians 12:7-10). Practically, it means that I run to Him when I’m
tempted and I run to Him when I fail, just like the sinful woman in Luke 7
and the lost son in Luke 15.
And we will fail. In fact, pursuing perfection can lead to a rigid way of life
bent on rule keeping. We need to remember: progress, not perfection.

TRUE ACCOUNTABILITY TRUE ACCOUNTABILITY
True accountability friendships are comprised of both truth and grace.
Grace is the acceptance we experience as we come into the light with
God and others. Truth is both my willingness to be authentic as well as
my willingness to receive direction from others.
There is great freedom and acceptance in the shared struggle. On the
other hand, in good support groups, there is an element of “tough
love”—speaking the truth to one another. Clear direction is available
through the 12 steps for those who want to get sober.
Good recovery groups exhibit both of these qualities. Nobody goes to
an AA support group, for example, followed by a brass band. People
enter meetings for the first time broken and beaten up. It doesn’t
matter whether one is an ex-con or the CEO of a Fortune 500 company.
Our accountability relationships must embrace both grace and truth. And
we need to go further than just tracking or informing of behavior. We
need to explore what is going on in our hearts—our emotions, passions,
dreams. Ultimately our sexual sin flows from our heart (Mark 7:21).
DEAL
WITH EMOTIONS DEAL WITH EMOTIONS
There is always a context to sexual struggle. Living in sexual integrity
means that we must become increasingly aware of our emotions. There
are two important reasons for this. First, the way that we process our
emotions will determine our progress in living in sexual integrity. Our
emotions will be processed somehow. We will either, identify, feel, and
express them or they will come out sideways in mostly destructive ways
such as anger, fear, resentment, or lust. Let me offer an example.
But there is a second and more important reason to actively process
feelings. Emotions are the windows into our hearts and minds. This
morning I realized that much of the fear and anxiety I was feeling
about my deadline had to do with being approved by others. I want
desperately for people to think I’m good at what I do. Over the years
I’ve based my identity on what I do and not on who God says I am. So
my feelings exposed some faulty and sinful beliefs. God says I will be
transformed by the renewing of my mind (Romans 12:2). The deepest

I realized I was feeling anxious, scared, and inadequate about getting

The temptation here is to quickly run to a purely intellectual solution to

While heart change is ultimately the goal in pursuing sexual integrity, I
must create room for lasting change by protecting myself in the midst
of sexual temptation. I must recognize my limits in terms of what I can
and cannot do.
For example, hotel rooms and I don’t mix very well because of the
temptation I experience in watching lustful content on TV. So, if I trav-
el, I need to make sure I’m either rooming with someone to whom I
can be accountable or staying with a friend. If neither of these options
is possible, I need to make a commitment to those I’m in a covenant
relationship with that when I arrive at the hotel I will immediately
disconnect the cable connection and bring it to the front desk. I’ve
had some looks of disbelief, to be sure, from hotel attendants, but it’s
more than worth it for me to avoid the temptation and to stay true to
what the Lord has called me to—the particular reason for the trip.
This is true freedom. I accept my limits and in surrender make choices
that will help to ensure continued connections with God and others.
Of course everybody has different weaknesses and vulnerabilities that
can potentially trip them up when it comes to remaining in sexual integ-
rity. It’s important to remember that while we can’t protect ourselves
from every temptation, constructing boundaries helps to set the table
for heart change.

The road to living in sexual integrity is not easy. It will take everything
you’ve got—not in your own strength, mind you, but in working in
partnership with the Lord and others. Finding those whom you can walk
through life with in grace and truth will take great intention on your
part.
First, I urge you to pray, pray, pray. Ask the Lord to lead you to others
who have the same heart to grow and walk in integrity.
Then look, look, look. Find a church where the pastor shares authentically
from his life. If the pastor leads from his own weakness, it is more likely
you will find those he shepherds who exhibit the same quality. Look for
others in Sunday school, in a singles group, in small groups at church,
and among believers you meet in your neighborhood or in your work
environment who you sense might be willing to walk in grace and truth
with you.
Take some risks. Jump in. Don’t be foolish, but as the Spirit leads, be will-
ing to be authentic and real with your own life. You may expose yourself
to being hurt, but you will also open up the possibility of having truly
transformational friendships.
